title: One recipe for sixty
hook: Split 60 into factors any way you like, down to primes. Does where you start matter?

knows: multiplication and division of whole numbers
what a prime number is (only 1 and itself divide it)
doesNotKnow: that every whole number above 1 factors into primes in only one way
the name fundamental theorem of arithmetic

misconception: A number can be broken into primes in different ways, depending on which factors you split off first.
objective: The learner can explain that different factor trees for 60 (6 x 10, 4 x 15, 2 x 30, ...) always end in the same primes 2, 2, 3, 5, and that every whole number above 1 has exactly one prime recipe apart from order.

claims.text: 60 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5, and every first split of 60 (2 x 30, 3 x 20, 4 x 15, 5 x 12, 6 x 10) ends in the primes 2, 2, 3, 5.
claims.source: 2x30 = 2x(5x(2x3)); 3x20 = 3x((2x2)x5); 4x15 = (2x2)x(3x5); 5x12 = 5x(3x(2x2)); 6x10 = (2x3)x(2x5). The stage computes the trees by trial division; recomputed with node.

claims.text: The 6 x 10 tree splits into 2 x 3 and 2 x 5; the 4 x 15 tree splits into 2 x 2 and 3 x 5.
Every whole number above 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors (the fundamental theorem of arithmetic).
claims.source: Euclid, Elements VII.30-32 and IX.14; Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, ch. 2, Theorem 2.

claims.text: 84 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7, whether you start from 4 x 21 or 6 x 14.
claims.source: Recall card in meta.json. Checked by the fact-checker: exhaustive factor trees of 84 give only {2,2,3,7}. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check.

recall.question: Ana factors 84 as 4 x 21 and Ben as 6 x 14. Both keep splitting down to primes. What do they find?
options: Different primes, because they started differently
The same primes but a different number of 2s
recall.why: Every whole number above 1 has exactly one prime recipe: 84 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7, whichever split you start with.
